title: [DRAFT - DO NOT DISTRIBUTE] Expert Validation: A Hierarchical Taxonomy of Biases in Human Decision-Making
description:
Researcher: Saima Sammad | Doctoral research / PhD | University of Bradford
Supervisory team: Professor Hassan Ugail and Dr Kamran Mahroof
Contact: {EMAIL} | Please respond by {RETURN_BY}

Expert review of a proposed taxonomy of biases in human decision-making: whether its categories are clear, relevant, distinct, comprehensive and practically usable.

Each category is presented on its own page, with its definition, dimensions and an illustrative example in front of you as you answer. You review in depth only the categories you select - every category page opens with a question that lets you skip straight to the next one.

Most experts review 2-4 categories, which takes about 25-35 minutes. Reviewing all ten takes 80-100 minutes.

validationRows: The name accurately represents the content of this category.

categories.title: Category 1: Personal Identity Biases
categories.definition: Bias arising from intrinsic or socially recognised personal identity characteristics that influence perceptions, evaluations and decision-making about individuals.
categories.example: A hiring panel rates an equally qualified candidate lower after learning that they hold non-citizen status, despite the candidate having unrestricted permission to work.
categories.note: Boundary note: “Socioeconomic Status” and “Marital Status”/“Parental Status” refer to an individual’s own demographic or social-position characteristics. Category 2 addresses related but distinct relational and behavioural constructs, including marital role expectations, parenting style, household composition and social-network affiliations.

categories.title: Category 2: Social and Relational Biases
categories.definition: Bias arising from social relationships, interpersonal interactions, network affiliations and perceived similarity in interests or values that influence perceptions, evaluations and decision-making.
categories.example: A manager gives a high-profile assignment to an employee from the same social network because they feel more comfortable with them.
categories.note: Boundary note: This category concerns relational standing, social connection and perceived interpersonal similarity rather than demographic status itself. Elective lifestyle and value-based dimensions are included only where they function as signals of affinity or social compatibility. Part F, Question 8 asks directly whether this consolidation is appropriate.

categories.title: Category 3: Professional and Educational Biases
categories.definition: Bias arising from professional roles, educational backgrounds, qualifications and career-related characteristics that influence perceptions of competence, credibility or suitability.
dimensions: Field of study (e.g., STEM vs. humanities)
categories.example: A panel rates a candidate more highly mainly because they attended a prestigious university.

categories.title: Category 4: Cognitive and Psychological Biases
categories.definition: Bias arising from psychological characteristics, cognitive tendencies, personality traits and behavioural patterns that influence judgement and decision-making.
dimensions: Individual risk orientation, including cautious, risk-taking and adventure-seeking tendencies
categories.example: An interviewer rates an introverted candidate as less capable of leadership, despite no evidence linking the two.
categories.note: Boundary note: This category addresses cognitive mechanisms, psychological traits and individual tendencies. “Individual risk orientation” is distinct from Category 5’s organisational risk-management practices and institutional risk tolerance.

categories.title: Category 5: Situational and Contextual Biases
categories.definition: Bias arising from situational, organisational or environmental conditions that influence perceptions, evaluations and decision-making.
dimensions: Organisational risk-management practices and institutional risk tolerance
categories.example: Under severe time pressure during a system outage, a manager relies on a stereotype about a team rather than reviewing the complete evidence.
categories.note: Boundary note: Organisational risk-management practices and institutional risk tolerance are contextual or organisational conditions. They are distinct from Category 4’s individual risk orientation.

categories.title: Category 6: Technological and Media Biases
categories.definition: Bias arising from technological systems, digital platforms and media environments that shape perceptions, evaluations and decision-making.
categories.example: A hiring manager interprets a limited online profile as evidence that an applicant lacks professional engagement.

categories.title: Category 7: Cultural and Regional Biases
categories.definition: Bias arising from cultural norms, traditions, regional identities and linguistic characteristics that influence perceptions, evaluations and decision-making.
dimensions: Generational cohort stereotypes (e.g., Generation Z, Millennials, Generation X or Baby Boomers)
categories.example: A customer-service applicant is judged as less capable because of their regional accent.
categories.note: Boundary note: “Generational cohort stereotypes” refers to culturally shared assumptions attached to a birth cohort as a social and cultural identity. This is distinct from “Age” in Category 1, which refers to chronological age as a demographic characteristic.

categories.title: Category 8: Health and Wellness Biases
categories.definition: Bias arising from physical or mental health conditions, disability, neurodiversity, wellbeing or other health-related characteristics that influence perceptions, evaluations and treatment of individuals.
dimensions: Dietary and wellness practices where interpreted as health-related
Body-image and weight-related health or wellbeing perceptions
categories.example: An employee with a disclosed long-term condition is passed over for promotion because of unsupported assumptions about reliability.
categories.note: Boundary note: “Body-image and weight-related health or wellbeing perceptions” concerns an underlying health/wellbeing characteristic or perception. Category 9 captures observable appearance-based stereotyping, assumptions or differential treatment.

categories.title: Category 9: Bias Manifestations and Indicators
categories.definition: Observable expressions of underlying bias reflected in behaviour, communication, judgements and decision-making practices that reveal biased attitudes or preferences.
dimensions: Appearance-based stereotyping, assumptions or differential treatment relating to physical appearance, height, weight, grooming, personal hygiene, fashion, personal style or body modification
categories.example: Two equivalent candidates receive different levels of questioning and evidence requirements because of an identity-related assumption.
categories.note: Structural note: Unlike Categories 1–8, this category represents manifestations rather than underlying sources. It captures observable evidence that an underlying bias has been expressed. Part F, Question 7 asks whether this should remain a category or be represented as a separate layer.

categories.title: Intersectionality (Cross-Cutting Property)
categories.definition: A cross-cutting relational property capturing compounded effects across two or more source categories and, where relevant, between multiple attributes within a single source category, producing overlapping or non-linear forms of disadvantage or privilege.
dimensions: And gender × ethnicity (compounding within Personal Identity). These combinations use attributes already represented within Categories 1–8
categories.example: An older employee with a disability is judged through the combined influence of age-related and disability-related assumptions in a way that cannot be adequately explained by either attribute independently.
categories.note: Structural note: Intersectionality is not a standalone source or manifestation. It is a cross-cutting relational property outside the numbered sequence. It primarily captures compounded effects across different source categories while also allowing multiple attributes within one source category to compound.

boundaryRows: Chronological age (Cat. 1) and generational cohort stereotypes (Cat. 7) are sufficiently distinguishable in practice.
A social or alumni tie (Cat. 2) and institutional prestige used as a competence signal (Cat. 3) are sufficiently distinguishable.
An individual’s own socioeconomic or marital status (Cat. 1) and relational constructs such as household composition (Cat. 2) are sufficiently distinguishable.
Individual risk orientation (Cat. 4) and organisational risk practice or leadership influence (Cat. 5) are sufficiently distinguishable.
A digital footprint (Cat. 6) and socioeconomic status (Cat. 1) are sufficiently distinguishable.
Body-image or weight as a health/wellbeing perception (Cat. 8) and appearance-based differential treatment (Cat. 9) are sufficiently distinguishable.
Where only differential treatment is observable, coding Category 9 alone without inferring a source category is workable.
wholeTaxonomyRows: The taxonomy has a clear and logical organising structure.
The taxonomy covers the major sources and forms of bias relevant to human decision-making.
The categories are sufficiently distinct and unnecessary duplication is limited.
The taxonomy is concise and avoids excessive complexity.
The taxonomy is robust enough to represent different decision-making domains.
The taxonomy can accommodate new or emerging bias dimensions.
The taxonomy helps explain how bias may arise, interact or become observable.
The distinction between underlying sources (Categories 1–8) and observable manifestations (Category 9) is conceptually clear.
Intersectionality is appropriately represented as a cross-cutting relational property.
A trained annotator could apply the taxonomy consistently to comparable narratives.
The taxonomy is suitable for dataset development and annotation.
The taxonomy is potentially useful for AI- or LLM-based bias detection.
The terminology is appropriate for an interdisciplinary academic audience.
The taxonomy offers a meaningful contribution beyond existing fragmented classifications.
openQuestions: G_STRENGTHS
What are the most important strengths of the proposed taxonomy?
G_WEAKNESSES
What are the most important weaknesses or risks?
G_MISSING
Are any important bias categories, dimensions, mechanisms or contexts missing? Please specify.
G_MERGE
Are any categories unnecessary, better merged, or better split?
G_HIERARCHY
Are any dimensions located at the wrong level, or under the wrong parent category?
G_CAT9
Should “Bias Manifestations and Indicators” remain Category 9, or be represented as a separate layer applied across all source categories?
G_CAT2

Category 2 absorbs elective lifestyle and value-based dimensions (hobbies, pet ownership, travel preferences, personal values, philanthropic interests) that were previously a standalone “Lifestyle and Values Biases” category. Is this consolidation appropriate, or should they be separated again?
G_INTERSECTIONALITY
Is intersectionality appropriately represented as a cross-cutting relational property rather than an additional category?
G_REFERENCES
What theoretical perspectives or key references should be added? (optional)
G_ESSENTIAL
What changes are essential before this taxonomy is used for dataset construction or AI-based bias detection?
